reference.source: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID) / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive Leigh syndrome caused by SURF1 mutations, in which a complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) assembly factor is deficient, giving isolated COX deficiency
Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with psychomotor regression, hypotonia, feeding and swallowing difficulty, and brainstem signs, often triggered or worsened by intercurrent illness
Brain MRI classically shows symmetrical T2-hyperintense lesions of the basal ganglia and brainstem, the imaging hallmark of Leigh syndrome
Elevated lactate in blood and cerebrospinal fluid supports a mitochondrial energy-generation defect, and CSF lactate can be raised even when blood is near-normal
SURF1 disease tends to produce a relatively consistent phenotype with hypertrichosis reported in some patients and a notably poor tolerance of anaesthesia and metabolic stress
Diagnosis rests on the MRI pattern, isolated COX deficiency on muscle histochemistry/biochemistry, and SURF1 sequencing; management is supportive with avoidance of catabolic stress
reference.pathophysiology: SURF1 encodes an assembly factor required for correct biogenesis of complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations reduce assembled, functional complex IV, impairing oxidative phosphorylation and cellular ATP production. Highly energy-dependent neurons, particularly in the basal ganglia and brainstem, undergo the characteristic subacute symmetrical necrosis of Leigh syndrome, with reactive lactate accumulation. Metabolic crises are commonly precipitated by infection, fasting, or other catabolic stress that further strains oxidative metabolism.
additionalDifferentials: Leigh syndrome from other nuclear or mitochondrial DNA mutations
Other complex IV assembly-factor defects (e.g. SCO2, COX10, COX15)
Biotinidase deficiency and biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease (treatable mimics)
Wilson disease and other basal ganglia disorders in older children
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis or infective encephalitis
additionalInvestigations: Blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate concentrations
Brain MRI to demonstrate symmetrical basal ganglia and brainstem lesions
Muscle biopsy with histochemistry showing cytochrome c oxidase deficiency and respiratory-chain enzymology
SURF1 gene sequencing and broader mitochondrial gene panels
Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids to exclude treatable metabolic mimics
Cardiac and ophthalmological assessment given multisystem mitochondrial involvement
redFlags: Acute neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness signalling a metabolic crisis
Brainstem dysfunction with respiratory irregularity or apnoea
Progressive bulbar involvement compromising airway and feeding safety
Anaesthetic exposure without mitochondrial precautions, risking decompensation
reference.prognosis: SURF1-related Leigh syndrome is typically progressive with a poor prognosis, and many affected children die in early childhood, often during metabolic crises, although the rate of decline varies. Care is supportive, aiming to prevent and manage crises and optimise nutrition and neurological function.
pitfalls: Overlooking treatable mimics of Leigh syndrome (such as biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease) before concluding an untreatable defect
Missing raised CSF lactate when blood lactate is normal
Failing to take mitochondrial anaesthetic and fasting precautions, precipitating crises
Attributing acute deterioration solely to infection without recognising metabolic decompensation
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
management: Prevent metabolic crises by avoiding fasting and catabolic stress and treating intercurrent illness promptly with adequate glucose-containing fluids
Offer supportive vitamin and cofactor supplementation such as thiamine, riboflavin and coenzyme Q10, recognising its unproven efficacy
Avoid mitochondrial-toxic drugs, particularly sodium valproate, and use anaesthesia cautiously given poor tolerance
Control seizures with anticonvulsants while avoiding valproate, and manage dystonia and spasticity
Provide nutritional support with gastrostomy feeding for swallowing difficulty and manage lactic acidosis during crises by treating the precipitant
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurology, metabolic, cardiology, ophthalmology, respiratory and palliative care
Offer genetic counselling with carrier and prenatal testing for this autosomal recessive SURF1 disorder
